title: The Holocaust
description: How Nazi antisemitism escalated from discrimination to the genocide of six million Jews, and how people resisted, survived and chose to remember.

notes.heading: Antisemitism in History
notes.body: The Holocaust did not come from nowhere. Antisemitism — hatred of and prejudice against Jewish people — had existed in Europe for centuries. In the Middle Ages, Jews were wrongly blamed for events like the Black Death, were expelled from many countries including England in 1290, and were often forced to live in separate districts and banned from many jobs. In the nineteenth century, old religious prejudice was joined by a new, pseudo-scientific racism that falsely claimed Jews were a separate and 'inferior' race. The Nazis took these old hatreds to a murderous extreme. Adolf Hitler made antisemitism the core of Nazi ideology, blaming Jewish people for everything from Germany's defeat in 1918 to both communism and capitalism — contradictory lies that scapegoated one small minority (less than 1% of Germany's population) for the nation's problems. Understanding this long history of prejudice helps us see how ordinary people could be taught to hate — and why challenging stereotypes and scapegoating matters in every society, including our own.

notes.heading: Escalating Persecution, 1933–1939
notes.body: Nazi persecution of Jewish Germans was deliberate and step by step. In April 1933, stormtroopers organised a boycott of Jewish shops and lawyers' and doctors' offices. Weeks later, Jewish people were dismissed from the civil service, and Jewish children were humiliated in schools. In 1935 the Nuremberg Laws removed German citizenship from Jews and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews; who counted as Jewish was defined by ancestry. Daily life became a maze of exclusions — from parks, swimming pools, universities, professions. In November 1938, after a Jewish teenager shot a German diplomat in Paris, the regime organised Kristallnacht, the 'Night of Broken Glass': synagogues burned, shop windows smashed, homes wrecked, nearly 100 people killed and 30,000 Jewish men sent to concentration camps. Afterwards the Jewish community was even forced to pay for the damage. Between 1933 and 1939 around 300,000 Jews fled Germany and Austria — families like Anne Frank's, who moved to Amsterdam. By 1939, Jewish Germans had been stripped of their rights, their property and their dignity — but worse was to come with the war.

notes.heading: Ghettos
notes.body: When Germany conquered Poland in 1939, it gained control of Europe's largest Jewish population — over three million people. The Nazis forced Jews in occupied countries into ghettos: sealed-off, walled districts of cities, guarded so no one could leave without permission. The largest was the Warsaw Ghetto, where around 400,000 people were crammed into an area meant for a fraction of that number. Conditions were appalling: families crowded into single rooms, food rations were below starvation level, disease spread, and in Warsaw tens of thousands died of hunger and illness even before deportations began. Yet people resisted dehumanisation in quiet, remarkable ways. Schools operated secretly. In the Łódź and Warsaw ghettos, musicians gave concerts and writers kept records. The historian Emanuel Ringelblum organised a secret archive in Warsaw — diaries, documents and children's drawings buried in milk cans and metal boxes — so that the truth would survive even if the people did not. 'Nothing is more precious to me than life itself,' one diarist wrote, 'so I want to live and to bear witness.'

notes.heading: The 'Final Solution' and the Camp System
notes.body: With the invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, Nazi persecution turned to genocide. Special killing units called Einsatzgruppen followed the armies east and shot around a million Jewish men, women and children in mass shootings, such as at Babi Yar near Kyiv, where nearly 34,000 people were murdered in two days. In January 1942, leading Nazis met at the Wannsee Conference to coordinate what they called the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question': the murder of all eleven million Jews in Europe. Killing centres were built in occupied Poland — Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Sobibor and others — where deportees from across Europe, transported in cattle trains, were murdered in gas chambers. Auschwitz was also a vast labour camp where prisoners were worked to death for German industry. Around six million Jews were murdered — two-thirds of Europe's Jews — including about 1.5 million children. The Nazis and their collaborators also murdered Roma, people with disabilities, Polish and Soviet civilians, political prisoners and others. The Holocaust was not an accident of war: it was a state-organised genocide, planned by leaders and carried out by hundreds of thousands of people.

notes.heading: Resistance: Armed and Spiritual
notes.body: Against impossible odds, Jews resisted. Armed resistance was desperately dangerous and almost always doomed — yet it happened. In April 1943, when the Nazis moved to finally empty the Warsaw Ghetto, a few hundred young fighters with smuggled pistols and homemade bombs fought back in the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, holding off German troops for nearly a month before the ghetto was burned down. There were revolts in the death camps themselves: at Sobibor and Treblinka in 1943, prisoners rose up and several hundred escaped; at Auschwitz in October 1944, prisoners blew up one of the crematoria. Jewish partisans, such as the Bielski brothers in the forests of Belarus, not only fought but rescued — their camp sheltered over 1,200 people, most of whom survived. Equally important was spiritual resistance: keeping religious faith, educating children in secret, writing diaries, making music and art — refusing to let the Nazis take away human dignity and culture. Anne Frank's diary, written in hiding in Amsterdam, is the most famous testimony of all: 'In spite of everything, I still believe that people are really good at heart.'

notes.heading: Liberation
notes.body: As the Allies advanced in 1944–45, they uncovered the camps. Soviet soldiers liberated Auschwitz on 27 January 1945, finding around 7,000 survivors too weak to have been forced onto the 'death marches' westwards, along with the possessions of the murdered — mountains of shoes, suitcases, human hair. British troops liberated Bergen-Belsen in April 1945 and found tens of thousands of starving, sick prisoners; the BBC reporter Richard Dimbleby's broadcast describing what he saw shocked the world. American forces liberated Dachau, Buchenwald and other camps. The survivors faced a long road: many had lost their entire families, and some who returned home met further hostility. About 250,000 survivors lived in 'Displaced Persons' camps for years; many emigrated to the new state of Israel (founded 1948), the USA, Britain and elsewhere. At the Nuremberg Trials of 1945–46, leading Nazis were prosecuted for crimes against humanity — a new legal concept born from the Holocaust. Liberation was not the end of the story: survivors rebuilt lives, bore witness, and ensured the world would know what happened.

notes.heading: Perpetrators, Bystanders, Rescuers — and Remembrance
notes.body: Historians ask us to think about three groups. Perpetrators were not only Hitler and the SS: genocide needed bureaucrats who organised trains, guards, and officials who stole property — ordinary people who chose to obey. Bystanders were the far larger group who knew, or could have known, and did nothing: in Germany, in occupied countries, and in Allied nations that turned away refugees — in 1939 the ship MS St Louis, carrying over 900 Jewish refugees, was refused entry to Cuba and the USA and forced back to Europe. Rescuers proved that choice existed: the Danish people helped almost all of Denmark's 8,000 Jews escape to Sweden in 1943; Oskar Schindler saved around 1,200 Jews by employing them in his factories; Irena Sendler smuggled about 2,500 children out of the Warsaw Ghetto. We study the Holocaust not only to honour the victims but because it shows where prejudice, scapegoating and indifference can lead. Holocaust Memorial Day (27 January) and survivors' testimony keep the memory alive. The lesson is for everyone: 'It happened, therefore it can happen again' — and each of us chooses, in small ways, whether to be a perpetrator, a bystander or an upstander.

flashcards.definition: Hatred of and prejudice against Jewish people. It existed in Europe for centuries before the Nazis turned it into state policy and genocide.
flashcards.example: In the Middle Ages Jews were expelled from England (1290) and falsely blamed for the Black Death.

flashcards.definition: A person or group unfairly blamed for problems they did not cause. The Nazis made Jews the scapegoat for Germany's defeat in 1918 and its economic crisis.
flashcards.example: Hitler blamed Jews for both communism and capitalism — contradictory lies.

flashcards.definition: Laws that stripped German Jews of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews, defining Jewish identity by ancestry.
flashcards.example: A German Jew could no longer vote, hold a German passport or marry a non-Jew.

flashcards.definition: The 'Night of Broken Glass', 9–10 November 1938: an organised nationwide attack on Jewish homes, shops and synagogues; nearly 100 people killed and 30,000 men sent to camps.
flashcards.example: Afterwards, around 300,000 Jews had fled Germany and Austria by 1939.

flashcards.definition: A sealed, guarded district where the Nazis forced Jews to live in occupied cities. The largest, in Warsaw, held around 400,000 people in desperate overcrowding and hunger.
flashcards.example: Emanuel Ringelblum's secret archive in Warsaw recorded ghetto life so the truth would survive.

flashcards.definition: The Nazi name for their plan, coordinated at the 1942 Wannsee Conference, to murder all the Jews of Europe. Around six million were killed, including 1.5 million children.
flashcards.example: Killing centres such as Auschwitz-Birkenau and Treblinka were built in occupied Poland.

flashcards.definition: The largest Nazi camp complex, in occupied Poland: both a killing centre, where about 1.1 million people were murdered, and a huge forced-labour camp. Liberated by the Soviet army on 27 January 1945.
flashcards.example: 27 January is now Holocaust Memorial Day, marking Auschwitz's liberation.

flashcards.definition: The armed Jewish resistance of April–May 1943, when young fighters held off German troops for nearly a month as the ghetto was destroyed.
flashcards.example: It was the largest single act of Jewish armed resistance during the Holocaust.

flashcards.definition: Non-violent defiance: keeping faith, secretly educating children, writing diaries and making art to preserve human dignity and culture under persecution.
flashcards.example: Anne Frank's diary, written in hiding in Amsterdam, became world-famous testimony.

flashcards.definition: Someone who knows about injustice and does nothing. Most people in Germany, occupied Europe and the Allied countries were bystanders rather than perpetrators or rescuers.
flashcards.example: In 1939 the refugee ship MS St Louis was turned away by Cuba and the USA.

flashcards.definition: Someone who risked their own safety to save Jews from the Holocaust, proving that moral choice existed even under terror.
flashcards.example: Oskar Schindler saved about 1,200 Jews; Denmark helped almost its whole Jewish community escape to Sweden.

flashcards.definition: Marked on 27 January, the anniversary of the liberation of Auschwitz, to remember the six million Jewish victims and others murdered, and to learn the lessons of the genocide.
flashcards.example: Survivors visit schools to share testimony so that the victims are never forgotten.

choices: Hatred of and prejudice against Jewish people
The study of ancient languages
Opposition to all religion
A political party in Germany
questions.explanation: Antisemitism means hatred of and prejudice against Jews. It existed in Europe for centuries before the Nazis, who made it the core of their ideology and, eventually, the basis of genocide.

questions.stem: Which of these shows that antisemitism existed in Europe long before the Nazis?
choices: The Nuremberg Laws of 1935
The expulsion of Jews from England in 1290 and false blame for the Black Death in the Middle Ages
The Wannsee Conference of 1942
The founding of Israel in 1948
questions.explanation: Medieval expulsions, forced separation and scapegoating — such as blaming Jews for the Black Death — show antisemitism's long history. The Nazis built on these old hatreds rather than inventing them.

questions.stem: What did the Nuremberg Laws of 1935 do?
choices: Gave Jewish Germans the right to vote
Stripped Jewish Germans of citizenship and banned marriage between Jews and non-Jews
Ended the persecution of Jewish people
Punished the organisers of Kristallnacht
questions.explanation: The Nuremberg Laws turned discrimination into law: Jews lost German citizenship, could not marry non-Jews, and were defined by ancestry. It was a key step in isolating them from German society.

questions.stem: Why is Kristallnacht (November 1938) seen as a turning point in Nazi persecution?
choices: It was the first time the persecution became openly violent and state-organised across the whole country
It was when Jewish Germans gained equal rights
It marked the start of the First World War
It was a protest organised by Jewish people against the Nazis
questions.explanation: Before 1938 persecution was mainly legal and economic. Kristallnacht was an organised nationwide pogrom — synagogues burned, about 100 people killed, 30,000 men sent to camps — showing violence was now official policy.

choices: Holiday camps for German workers
Sealed, guarded districts of cities in occupied Europe where Jews were forced to live in overcrowded, starving conditions
Underground resistance tunnels
Prisons for captured Allied soldiers
questions.explanation: From 1939 the Nazis confined Jews in walled ghettos such as Warsaw, where around 400,000 people were crammed into a small district. Overcrowding, hunger and disease killed tens of thousands.

questions.stem: What was decided at the Wannsee Conference of January 1942?
choices: The surrender of Germany
The coordination of the 'Final Solution' — the plan to murder all the Jews of Europe
The founding of the United Nations
The division of Germany after the war
questions.explanation: At Wannsee, senior Nazis and government officials coordinated the 'Final Solution to the Jewish Question': the deportation and murder of Europe's eleven million Jews. It shows the genocide was planned by the state.

questions.stem: Approximately how many Jewish people were murdered in the Holocaust?
choices: Sixty thousand
Six hundred thousand
Six million
Sixty million
questions.explanation: Around six million Jews — two-thirds of Europe's Jewish population, including about 1.5 million children — were murdered. The Nazis and their collaborators also killed Roma, people with disabilities and many others.

questions.stem: What was the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising?
choices: A strike by German factory workers
The armed Jewish resistance of April 1943, when young fighters held off German forces for nearly a month as the ghetto was destroyed
The liberation of Auschwitz by Soviet troops
A protest against food rationing in Berlin
questions.explanation: In April 1943, a few hundred young Jews with smuggled weapons fought the Germans rather than be deported to death camps. Though defeated, it was the largest act of Jewish armed resistance of the Holocaust.

questions.stem: Which of these is the best example of spiritual resistance?
choices: Blowing up a railway line
Joining the German army to spy on it
Secretly educating children, keeping religious faith and writing diaries to preserve dignity and culture
Organising an armed revolt in a camp
questions.explanation: Spiritual resistance meant refusing to be dehumanised: secret schools, religious practice, music, art and diaries like Anne Frank's. It preserved identity and hope where armed resistance was almost impossible.

choices: British troops
American troops
The Polish government-in-exile
Soviet troops
questions.explanation: The Soviet Red Army liberated Auschwitz on 27 January 1945, finding around 7,000 survivors left behind. British forces liberated Bergen-Belsen and Americans liberated Dachau and Buchenwald.

questions.stem: What did the fate of the refugee ship MS St Louis in 1939 reveal about the wider world?
choices: That all countries welcomed Jewish refugees
That bystander nations also failed the Jews — Cuba and the USA refused entry to over 900 refugees, forcing the ship back to Europe
That refugees were only accepted by Germany
That the war had already ended
questions.explanation: The St Louis carried over 900 Jewish refugees who were refused entry to Cuba and the USA and had to return to Europe, where many later died in the Holocaust. It shows indifference beyond Germany's borders.

questions.stem: What do the actions of Oskar Schindler, Irena Sendler and the Danish people in 1943 demonstrate?
choices: That resistance was impossible under the Nazis
That moral choice existed even under terror — rescuers saved thousands of Jewish lives at great personal risk
That only soldiers could help the persecuted
That the Allies organised all rescue efforts
questions.explanation: Schindler saved about 1,200 Jews, Sendler smuggled roughly 2,500 children from the Warsaw Ghetto, and Denmark evacuated almost its entire Jewish community to Sweden — proof that individuals and nations could choose to act.

questions.stem: A historian writes: 'The Holocaust was not carried out by monsters but within a modern state by ordinary people.' What does this mean?
choices: Only a few evil individuals were involved
Genocide required not just leaders but thousands of ordinary officials, guards and bureaucrats who chose to obey, while millions more stood by
No one was responsible for the Holocaust
The German state had no role in the killings
questions.explanation: The Holocaust was organised like a state project: train timetables, paperwork and property theft all needed ordinary people doing their jobs. Understanding this warns us how bureaucracies and obedience can enable evil.

questions.stem: Why do historians describe the escalation of Nazi persecution as 'step by step' rather than a single decision?
choices: Because the boycott of 1933, the Nuremberg Laws of 1935, Kristallnacht in 1938, ghettos from 1939 and mass murder from 1941 each radicalised the persecution further
Because persecution never changed between 1933 and 1945
Because the Nazis were unsure whether they disliked Jewish people
Because Jewish people chose to move into ghettos
questions.explanation: Each stage — boycott, laws, pogrom, ghetto, genocide — went further than the last, often when the world failed to react. This gradual radicalisation is a key lesson in how genocide becomes possible.

questions.stem: Why is studying the Holocaust still important today?
choices: It is only relevant to historians of Germany
It shows where prejudice, scapegoating and indifference can lead, and reminds us that each person can choose to be an upstander rather than a bystander
It proves that genocide could never happen again
It is useful only for remembering military battles
questions.explanation: The Holocaust teaches the consequences of hatred left unchallenged and the power of individual moral choice. Remembrance — through Holocaust Memorial Day and survivors' testimony — keeps those lessons alive.
